question about replication in databases. does postgres allow semi synchronous replication? Also how do I setup say a semi synchronous replication in rds with 4 replicas with one warm standby

Gemini said

Does PostgreSQL Allow Semi-Synchronous Replication?

Yes. In open-source (native) PostgreSQL, semi-synchronous replication is fully supported and configured using a combination of two parameters: synchronous_commit and synchronous_standby_names.

By setting synchronous_standby_names to a quorum-based syntax, such as:

SQL
synchronous_standby_names = 'ANY 1 (replica1, replica2, replica3)'

And keeping synchronous_commit = on (or setting it to remote_write), you instruct the primary database to proceed with a transaction commit as soon as at least one of the listed replicas acknowledges receiving the Write-Ahead Log (WAL) data. This provides a balance of high durability (guaranteeing data lives in at least two places) without waiting for every single replica to reply.

The Catch with AWS RDS

While native Postgres allows you to adjust these configurations freely, AWS RDS does not allow you to manually modify synchronous_standby_names for standard Read Replicas. RDS fully manages the replication stream and network topology, so modifying these parameters directly in a custom DB Parameter Group is restricted.

However, AWS provides a specific architecture built exactly for this use case called an RDS Multi-AZ DB Cluster.

How an RDS Multi-AZ DB Cluster Works

Unlike a standard Multi-AZ instance (which uses block-level storage replication to a non-readable standby), a Multi-AZ DB Cluster uses PostgreSQL's native streaming replication configured semi-synchronously across three Availability Zones (AZs). It provisions:

  • 1 Primary Writer

  • 2 Readable Standby Instances (Readers)

A transaction is only committed on the primary after at least one of the readable standbys acknowledges the write to its local storage (a 2-out-of-3 quorum).

How to Set Up 4 Replicas with One Warm Standby in RDS

To achieve your exact goal of having semi-synchronous durability, a warm standby for failover, and a total of 4 readable replicas, you must combine an RDS Multi-AZ DB Cluster with standard asynchronous Read Replicas.

Step 1: Create the Multi-AZ DB Cluster (The Core)

This step establishes your semi-synchronous foundation and your warm standby tier.

  1. Open the Amazon RDS Console.

  2. Click Create database.

  3. Choose PostgreSQL as your engine.

  4. Under Deployment options, select Multi-AZ DB cluster (do not choose Multi-AZ DB instance).

  5. Configure your instance sizes, storage, and connectivity parameters.

  6. Click Create database.

What this gives you: You now have 1 Writer and 2 Replicas that are bound by semi-synchronous replication. Both replicas are readable. If the primary dies, RDS automatically fails over to one of these two nodes (acting as your warm/hot standby layer) with zero data loss in typically under 35 seconds.

Step 2: Add 2 Additional Read Replicas (The Scale-Out)

To hit your target of 4 replicas total, you will spin up two additional standard read replicas. These will replicate asynchronously from the cluster's primary writer.

  1. In the RDS Console, select your newly created Multi-AZ DB cluster writer instance.

  2. Click Actions -> Create read replica.

  3. Configure the destination AZ/Region and instance options.

  4. Repeat this process to create a second read replica.

Final Architecture Breakdown

Node TypeReplication TypeRole
Primary InstanceN/A (Source)Handles all application writes.
Cluster Standby 1Semi-SynchronousReadable replica + Active failover target (Warm Standby).
Cluster Standby 2Semi-SynchronousReadable replica + Backup failover target.
Read Replica 3AsynchronousDedicated to read-scaling.
Read Replica 4AsynchronousDedicated to read-scaling.

With this setup, your application writes are safely protected by a semi-synchronous quorum across your primary cluster, while your read traffic can be distributed across all 4 available replica endpoints.

An Alternative to Consider: Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL

If your architecture allows for a change in database type, Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL handles this topology natively and more efficiently.

Instead of traditional WAL streaming, Aurora uses a cloud-native shared storage layer that replicates data 6 ways across 3 AZs synchronously. You can spin up to 15 Aurora Replicas that all read from this same shared storage layer. Because they share storage, replication lag is virtually non-existent (typically <20ms), and you can explicitly assign failover tiers (Tier 0 to Tier 15) to designate exactly which replica acts as your dedicated warm standby.

But Aurora is not postgres, correct? And isnt it costlier than rds?

Gemini said

You’ve hit on two very common—and completely fair—perceptions. Let’s break down the nuance of both, because the answers are a bit of a "yes and no" paradox.

1. Is Aurora "Real" Postgres?

To your application: Yes, it is.

Under the hood: No, it’s a heavily modified fork.

AWS calls it "Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL-Compatible Edition." Here is what that actually means:

  • The Wire & Features (Standard Postgres): It uses the exact same SQL dialect, supports the same extensions (like pgvector or PostGIS), and uses standard PostgreSQL drivers. Your application won't know the difference; it thinks it's talking to regular Postgres.

  • The Storage & Replication (Proprietary AWS): AWS stripped out the standard open-source storage engine and replaced it with a cloud-native, distributed, log-structured storage system. Instead of writing data locally and streaming WAL logs to replicas over the network, Aurora writes data to 6 different storage nodes across 3 Availability Zones simultaneously.

So, it's Postgres at the feature/query layer, but completely custom at the infrastructure layer.

2. Is Aurora Costlier Than RDS?

Instance-for-instance? Yes. Aurora compute instances carry roughly a 20% price premium over the exact equivalent RDS instances.

For your specific setup (4 Replicas)? It might actually be cheaper.

This sounds counterintuitive, but it comes down to how storage is billed for replicas:

The Storage Multiplier on RDS

On standard RDS, every single read replica requires its own completely independent storage volume.

  • If you have 1 Primary + 4 Replicas, and your database is 1 TB, you have to provision and pay for 5 TB of storage (1 TB for each node).

The Shared Storage Advantage on Aurora

On Aurora, all replicas share the exact same storage volume.

  • If you have 1 Primary + 4 Replicas, and your database is 1 TB, you only pay for 1 TB of storage total. The replicas just point to the same shared virtual disk.

The Math: A Quick TCO Comparison

Imagine a 1 TB database on mid-sized instances (db.r6g.xlarge) with 4 replicas:

Cost ComponentAmazon RDS (Postgres)Amazon Aurora (Postgres)
Compute CostBase price (5 instances)~20% Higher (5 instances)
Storage Cost5 TB (Paid per provisioned GB)1 TB (Paid only for what you use)
I/O FeesIncluded (up to gp3 baseline)Variable ($0.20 per million I/Os on Standard)

The Verdict: If your database has moderate I/O, Aurora often wins on price once you scale past 2 or 3 replicas because the storage savings completely wipe out the 20% compute premium. However, if your database is tiny in storage but aggressively hammers the disk with millions of small read/write I/O operations every minute, Aurora Standard's I/O charges can make it significantly more expensive.

(Note: AWS does offer an "Aurora I/O-Optimized" tier that removes I/O charges entirely in exchange for a flat price increase, which makes budgeting highly predictable for high-I/O workloads).

Does your specific workload lean more toward heavy storage volume, or intense, non-stop read/write traffic?

You said

how is this done in clickhouse?

Gemini said

ClickHouse handles replication entirely differently than traditional OLTP databases like PostgreSQL. Because ClickHouse is a columnar OLAP database, it does not use a rigid "Primary-Replica" instance topology. Instead, it uses a multi-master, table-level replication model coordinated by ClickHouse Keeper (or ZooKeeper).

Every replica in ClickHouse is capable of accepting both reads and writes.

1. Does ClickHouse Allow Semi-Synchronous Replication?

Yes. By default, ClickHouse replication is asynchronous. When you insert data into one replica, it acknowledges the write immediately, and other replicas pull the data in the background.

However, you can achieve semi-synchronous behavior using the insert_quorum setting.

  • Setting insert_quorum = 2 dictates that an INSERT statement will only return a "Success" acknowledgment to your application after the data has been written to the local replica plus at least one other replica.

  • If the quorum isn't met within a specified window (controlled by insert_quorum_timeout), the write fails and rolls back.

2. Setting Up 4 Replicas with One "Warm Standby"

Because all ClickHouse replicas are active and identical, you don't designate a node as a "warm standby" via configuration files. Instead, you create a 4-replica cluster and enforce the "warm standby" behavior via your network routing layer.

Here is the step-by-step implementation:

Step 1: Set up ClickHouse Keeper

Before configuring your database nodes, you need a coordination tier. Deploy a 3-node ClickHouse Keeper cluster. This lightweight service manages the replication queues and parts state.

Step 2: Define your 4-Replica Cluster

In your ClickHouse configuration XML (e.g., /etc/clickhouse-server/config.d/cluster.xml), define a single shard containing all 4 of your database nodes.

XML
<remote_servers>
    <analytics_cluster>
        <shard>
            <internal_replication>true</internal_replication>
            <replica><host>clickhouse-node1</host><port>9000</port></replica>
            <replica><host>clickhouse-node2</host><port>9000</port></replica>
            <replica><host>clickhouse-node3</host><port>9000</port></replica>
            <replica><host>clickhouse-node4</host><port>9000</port></replica> </shard>
    </analytics_cluster>
</remote_servers>

Step 3: Create a Replicated Table

Log into ClickHouse and create your table using the ReplicatedMergeTree engine. This engine automatically talks to Keeper to sync data.

SQL
CREATE TABLE my_db.events ON CLUSTER analytics_cluster
(
    event_id UInt64,
    event_time DateTime,
    event_name String
)
ENGINE = ReplicatedMergeTree('/clickhouse/tables/{shard}/events', '{replica}')
PARTITION BY toYYYYMM(event_time)
ORDER BY event_id;

Step 4: Enforce Semi-Synchronous Behavior

To ensure your writes are semi-synchronous, pass the quorum settings during your INSERT operations (or set them globally in the user profile):

SQL
SET insert_quorum = 2;
SET insert_quorum_timeout = 30000; -- 30 seconds

With insert_quorum = 2 on a 4-node cluster, you guarantee that your data safely lives on at least two distinct physical servers before a write is confirmed.

Step 5: Isolate the "Warm Standby"

Because clickhouse-node4 is physically identical to the other three, it will continuously pull replication parts in the background. To make it act as a warm standby:

  1. For Reads: Configure your application load balancer (or your ClickHouse Distributed engine table) to route SELECT queries only to nodes 1, 2, and 3.

  2. For Writes: Route INSERT queries only to nodes 1, 2, and 3. Node 4 will naturally pull the data via Keeper.

  3. Failover: If Node 1, 2, or 3 goes offline, your load balancer alters its health checks and begins routing active production traffic to Node 4.

The ClickHouse Storage & Cost Reality

Tieing back to your question about RDS vs. Aurora storage costs:

  • Standard Open-Source ClickHouse: Operates like RDS. If you have 4 replicas and a 1 TB dataset, each node must have its own NVMe/SSD drive. You will pay for 4 TB of provisioned storage.

  • ClickHouse Cloud (and Modern Shared Object Storage VFS): Operates like Aurora. Modern ClickHouse setups decouple compute from storage by utilizing cloud object storage (like AWS S3) via a feature called Virtual File System (VFS) or SharedMergeTree. All 4 of your ClickHouse compute instances point to a single, shared dataset sitting on S3.

If you use ClickHouse with an S3-backed VFS storage policy, your storage cost stays at a flat 1 TB, and adding replicas 2, 3, and 4 only incurs the cost of the raw compute instances—making a 4-replica architecture incredibly economical.
